node.label: James Vernon
node.date_label: Politics and the People 1993 · “Who's Afraid of the ‘Linguistic Turn’?” 1994 · Re-reading the Constitution (ed.) 1996 · review of Lawrence 1999 · “The Ethics of Hunger” 2005 · Hunger 2007 · The Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity (ed., with Gunn) 2011 · Distant Strangers 2014 · “The History of Britain Is Dead” 2016 · Modern Britain 2017 · “The Worlding of Britain” 2018 · “Heathrow and the Making of Neoliberal Britain” 2021
node.description: A British historian (Manchester, then Berkeley) who credited Patrick Joyce as an adviser and continuing influence. Politics and the People (1993) argued that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed: 'The invention of democracy in England was then a sham'; popular constitutionalism, not class, was its master narrative, and the identities it found were 'not done justice by Patrick Joyce's "family of populisms"' (all as quoted by Tilly, 1994). He answered social history's critics with 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' (1994) and gathered the new political history in Re-reading the Constitution (1996). Tilly found 'shrill bravado' and 'softcore solipsism'; Lawrence asked whether popular politics had declined, and Vernon found Lawrence's realism 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999). Hunger (2007) sought, as he told Oddy in 2009, to understand hunger 'as a cultural category not a biological condition'; Distant Strangers (2014) made a 'society of strangers' the modern social condition; from 2016 he proposed 'a global history of Britain concerned with how the world made Britain'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: James Vernon (b. 1965); Politics and the People: A Study in English Political Culture, c.1815–1867 (1993); 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"? The Politics of Social History and Its Discontents' (Social History 19, 1994); ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); review of Lawrence, Speaking for the People (Reviews in History, 1999); 'The Ethics of Hunger and the Assembly of Society' (American Historical Review, 2005); Hunger: A Modern History (2007); with Simon Gunn, eds, The Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity in Imperial Britain (2011); Distant Strangers: How Britain Became Modern (2014); 'More Secondary Modern than Post-modern: Patrick Joyce and the Peculiarities of Liberal Modernity in Britain' (Cultural and Social History, 2016); Modern Britain, 1750 to the Present (2017; 2nd ed. 2025); 'The Worlding of Britain' (Journal of British Studies, 2018); 'Heathrow and the Making of Neoliberal Britain' (Past and Present, 2021). Readers: Charles Tilly (1994); Jon Lawrence (1994; 2010); Derek Oddy (2008); David Craig (2016).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-22 (data/extension-2026/languages-of-class-2026-10-22/evidence-joyce-vernon-lawrence.md, Part B): Politics and the People only in seven paged passages (pp. 49, 103, 107, 297, 335, 336, 338) as quoted by Tilly (1994), whose review was read in full; the 1994 Social History article in its metadata only (its subtitle answers Mayfield and Thorne); Re-reading the Constitution in its contents; the 1999 review of Lawrence and Lawrence's 2010 response in full; the 2005 AHR opening; Hunger in its publisher description, Oddy's review and Vernon's 2009 response (all read); the 2011 introduction with Gunn in full; Distant Strangers and Modern Britain in publisher descriptions and Craig's 2016 review; the 2016 and 2021 (Heathrow) abstracts; the 2018 JBS essay. The adviser relation to Joyce rests on the 2011 acknowledgments ('As an adviser he was a constant catalyst'). Unread: the body of every book and the 1994 article; Lawrence's 1994 review beyond its title. A Foucault influence is not drawn: Tilly notes the 1993 epigraph and the 2005 article opens on Donzelot, but Craig (2016) says Distant Strangers does not employ liberal governmentality. Born 2 March 1965 (Wikidata); University of Manchester (Reviews in History, 1999); professor of history, University of California, Berkeley (2011 volume; Wikidata).

proposed_edges.relationship: Politics and the People (1993): between 1832 and 1867 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed, so that 'the invention of democracy in England was then a sham' (as quoted by Tilly, 1994); Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered the 'new cultural history of British politics' (his phrase, 2004)
proposed_edges.map_label: The closure of the public sphere, 1993–96
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pp. 107 and 336 as quoted by Tilly (1994, read in full; the book unread): 'despite all the legislation which historians have traditionally seen as heralding a brave new world of mass democratic politics … this period witnessed a marked decline in people's ability to shape the political appeals available to them as the official political subject was redefined in the image of print'; 'The invention of democracy in England was then a sham'. Re-reading the Constitution: contents read (Epstein, Fulcher, Wahrman, Burney, Antony Taylor, Joyce, Clark). The phrase 'the new cultural history of British politics' from his 2004 review of Epstein (opening read). Eley and Nield (2000, p. 8, read) on his 'neglected traces'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Popular constitutionalism as the 'master narrative' of English politics; civic landscapes 'read as cultural texts in themselves' (1993, as quoted by Tilly); 'Who's Afraid of the "Linguistic Turn"?' answered social history's 'discontents' (1994)
proposed_edges.map_label: Who's afraid of the linguistic turn? 1993–94
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pp. 49 and 297 as quoted by Tilly (1994, read in full): 'civic landscapes can be read as cultural texts in themselves, texts of equal significance to the ceremonies and other symbolic practices that were staged upon them' (p. 49); 'popular constitutionalism' as 'the "master narrative" of English politics at least through 1867' (Tilly, p. 266). Tilly notes that Vernon 'neither argues that their meanings reside entirely in discourse nor subordinates them to language' (p. 266). The 1994 Social History article is unread: its title and subtitle answer Mayfield and Thorne (1992), and nothing of its argument is stated here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his 2009 response to Oddy, Vernon explained that he had wanted to understand hunger 'as a cultural category not a biological condition'; in existing histories 'hunger often remains an unproblematic category … presented as a self-evident material condition' (2005); 'the social' as something assembled, not given
proposed_edges.map_label: Hunger and the assembly of society, 2005–09
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: AHR 2005 opening (read): 'Hunger often remains an unproblematic category in these histories, presented as a self-evident material condition'; the epigraph from Donzelot on 'the social'. Response to Oddy (Reviews in History, 2009, read in full): 'Simply put, I wanted to understand hunger as a cultural category not a biological condition'; he is 'interested though in historicizing the construction and politics of that knowledge'. Harvard description of Hunger (read). A critique of the self-evidence of material categories in social history, not of the field as such.

proposed_edges.relationship: 'A global history of Britain … not because of that old imperial conceit that Britain made the world, but because the world made Britain' (2016; Modern Britain, 2017); against 'Britain and the world' as a field that can 'reanimate an Anglo world in which white men invariably occupy center stage' (2018); neoliberalism seen from Heathrow (2021)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own words: History Australia abstract (2016, read): 'I propose a global history of modern Britain around an account of the rise, demise and reinvention of a liberal political economy … This history of Britain is then a global story, not because of that old imperial conceit that Britain made the world, but because the world made Britain.' JBS 2018 forum (his section read): an imperial history of the British world can 'reanimate an Anglo world in which white men invariably occupy center stage'; 'a global history of Britain concerned with how the world made Britain'. Heathrow abstract (2021, read): neoliberalism 'less about the global flow of ideas and capital than the local social formations and labour regimes engendered by changing forms of accumulation'. Cambridge descriptions of Modern Britain (2017; 2025).

proposed_edges.relationship: Speaking for the People's attempt to combine 'material context with discursive representation' is 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' and reads 'as though it has been written by a schizophrenic'; census and survey data are treated as unproblematic (1999)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Reviews in History 69 (read in full): the book attempts 'a new methodology that combines material context with discursive representation'; it is 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed', treating class and locality as material realities in some chapters and discursive constructs in others; Lawrence treats census and survey data as unproblematic, ignoring how such sources helped constitute the social domain; the book 'singularly fails to move from the local to the national'. Vernon counts himself among the 'postmodernist revisionists' Lawrence sets himself against. Lawrence's 2010 response is drawn as jon_lawrence → james_vernon.

proposed_edges.relationship: The 'new cultural history of British politics' (2004); hunger as a cultural category (2007); the 'cultural turn' and 'imperial turn' as his declared frame, to which Oddy objected and which Craig saw in Distant Strangers' debt to cultural studies
proposed_edges.map_label: Cultural history of politics and hunger, 2004–14
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own phrase from the 2004 review of Epstein (opening read): 'the new cultural history of British politics'. Oddy (2008, read in full): Vernon 'is a modern cultural historian' who invokes 'the cultural turn' or 'the imperial turn'; 'British society has been studied effectively without such jargon'; Vernon's response (2009, read) that the review misreads his use of the cultural and imperial turns. Craig (2016, read) on Distant Strangers' debt to cultural studies and its doubt of modernity as a singular condition. Hunger: Harvard description.
